source.title: On the Optimal Batch Size for Byzantine-Robust Distributed Learning
source.authors: Yi-Rui Yang; Chang-Wei Shi; Wu-Jun Li

record.tranche_reason: Tests how batch size and normalized momentum affect image-classification accuracy in Byzantine-robust distributed training, an extension of the batch-size and training-recipe claims to Byzantine attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper's directly relevant results are its own ResNet-20/CIFAR-10 test-accuracy tables varying batch size, attack fraction, aggregator, and normalization. Cited results about large-batch training from other papers are not rows. Training accuracy and train-test gaps are not reported.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures V5's held-out accuracy outcome while varying batch size at a fixed 160-epoch budget, extending the comparison to Byzantine-robust distributed training. It is not an original source for V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: their convergence-bound analysis and experiments indicate that the optimal batch size increases with Byzantine-worker fraction, and normalized momentum can alleviate accuracy losses at large batches. They report comparable performance under bit-flipping failure and better best accuracy under crafted attacks except KR/FoE, where both methods fail. The theoretical result concerns convergence bounds, not a theorem about held-out accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: Byzantine-robust distributed training with local momentum and robust aggregation; evaluates batch-size sweeps and adds normalized momentum. It is an extension into Byzantine attacks, not the original standard-training comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Test accuracy depends on batch size, Byzantine fraction or attack type, and robust aggregator. Under FoE with KR, both methods remain at 10.00% for all tested batch sizes; under no attack, larger batches reduce accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: The theoretical optimal batch size minimizes an upper bound on expected gradient norm; it increases with Byzantine-worker fraction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The batch size optimizing a nonconvex convergence bound increases with the fraction of Byzantine workers under the stated assumptions.

record.problems: Only one architecture and dataset are tested. Reported results are best final test accuracies selected from eight initial learning rates; no uncertainty estimates are stated. Training error is not reported, so train-test gap is not measured. Experiments use Byzantine-robust distributed learning and do not evaluate standard single-model training.
record.rows_left_out: None of the directly relevant table results were omitted. Tables 2–5 report ByzSGDnm results alongside ByzSGDm; separate ByzSGDnm rows are not cataloged because the claim version concerns the batch-size generalization effect, and the paper's ByzSGDnm comparison is a proposed-method result rather than an additional test of that version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps and performance beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers and their tuning regimes.

Language models, longer training, learning-rate scaling with warmup, and regularization changes. Only ResNet-20/CIFAR-10 is tested; no training accuracy is reported to distinguish optimization failure from a larger train-test gap.
Dropout, training-set size, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removal of memorized versus randomly selected examples.

missing.locator: Table 1; δ=0 repeated in Table 2 and δ=3/8 repeated in Table 4

record.verdict_notes: All recorded values match the supplied tables. Each sweep reports best final test accuracy selected across eight initial learning rates, without uncertainty estimates; the relevant baseline is a smaller batch within that sweep. Fixed epochs keep non-Byzantine gradient computations fixed within each attack fraction, but that computation budget changes across fractions. The declared omission of normalized-momentum sweeps is consequential: their within-method batch-size effects also bear on V5's recipe-adaptation clause, although their omission is already disclosed in rows_left_out. Table 5 additionally contains an inconsistency: GM/ByzSGDnm's Best entry is 90.00%, while its 128×8 entry is 90.99%.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width beyond interpolation threshold and test error as a function of width.
Language models, comparison to small batches under a fixed epoch budget across other models, and the cited alternative recipe changes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train-test gap.

tranche.reason: Tests fixed-epoch batch-size effects on held-out accuracy in the new setting of Byzantine-robust distributed learning.

source_check.notes: Accuracies are best final test accuracies selected across eight initial learning rates; uncertainty estimates are not reported. R14 duplicates R3, and the KR/FoE result describes complete failure.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: ResNet20 on CIFAR-10 under the tested Byzantine attacks and aggregators
reader_labels.reason: The direction and magnitude of batch-size effects vary by attack fraction and aggregator; with no attack, test accuracy declines at larger batches (R1, R4, R5), while under attacks the best batch is often larger but not uniformly increasing across the sweep (R2–R9, R14–R19). The study uses 160 epochs for all settings, so it does not test whether longer training removes the penalty.
